title: Cost and Compute Tradeoff Engineering: Visual Guide
outline: Title: Cost and Compute Tradeoff Engineering: Visual Guide

1. Where The Money Sits | the same five backbone stages from lesson 1, viewed twice — once through lessons 1-2 (contracts, source of truth vs derived copies, freshness SLAs, hit rate and golden sets) and once through this lesson's cost levers | every lever in this lesson is applied to a derived copy, which is exactly why it is safe to pull: a wrong tier, quantization level or precompute is recoverable by a rebuild

2. The Tiering Ledger | six embedding generations of 400 GB each, cycled hot / warm / cold with the monthly line item, the cut versus all-hot, and warnings when the serving or rollback copy is mis-tiered | tier by measured access and test restore time, not just price — archiving everything past the rollback window cuts this line by about two-thirds, but the current and previous generations must stay reachable

3. Precompute Break-Even | a reads-per-day slider against a rebuild-cadence slider for a 300 ms dashboard query, plus the four framework questions as toggles that overrule the arithmetic | volume decides only after the framework does: query-dependent values cannot be precomputed at all, a 100 ms budget forces precompute regardless of volume, and the break-even point moves with how fresh you promised the value would be

4. Recall Per Dollar | five quantization configurations at 5M, 10M and 12M vectors with a recall-floor slider, showing measured recall, serving memory and the replica count each implies | pick the cheapest configuration above your recall floor, remember that memory saved is replicas saved, and treat a configuration with no measured recall as a guess rather than a point on the frontier

5. Rebuild Payback Math | four evidence presets (vendor benchmark, golden set overall, golden set per class, a marginal reading) driving a gain and traffic-share calculator that returns better answers per day and payback in days | the trigger comes before the arithmetic — a benchmark chart is not evidence and a sub-threshold gain is not measurably better — and a gain concentrated in one class is re-embedded class-gated first because the same gain over a smaller rebuild is a different decision
